491.quote_or_event: After Guru Gobind Singh sent him to the Punjab in 1708, Banda Singh Bahadur did not strike at once at Sirhind, the seat of the Mughal governor Wazir Khan. He first took Samana, Sadhaura and other towns, following a long, roundabout route while he waited for Sikhs from the Doaba and Majha to join him, and only then attacked Sirhind, which fell after the battle of Chappar Chiri in May 1710.
491.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism records that Banda Singh deliberately delayed his main blow until he had gathered strength and secured the ground around his target.
491.tie_back: The Kural says not to move against an enemy, or to belittle him, until one has found ground from which to surround and overcome him; Banda Singh likewise waited and built a base before attacking Sirhind.
491.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Banda Singh Bahadur', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
491._accuracy_note: A genuine historical parallel for patient, ground-first strategy, but it concerns a commander's campaign rather than a teaching of the Gurus, and the source stresses gathering forces more than choosing terrain.

492.quote_or_event: “The Sanctuary of the Lord's Feet is my fortress and battlement.”
492.explanation: Guru Arjan names God's protection as his fort and rampart, the secure position from which he faces every threat.
492.tie_back: The Kural says even the strong gain much by fighting from a fortified position; Guru Arjan names the one fortress Gurbani trusts above all others.
492.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 742, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
492._accuracy_note: The fortress image matches closely, but Gurbani's fortress is spiritual refuge in God, not a military stronghold.

493.quote_or_event: “My True Guru is the power of the powerless.”
493.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that those who have no strength of their own become strong once they take shelter with the Guru.
493.tie_back: The Kural says even the weak overcome their enemies when they take the right position and guard themselves; Gurbani says the powerless gain power by taking the Guru as their refuge.
493.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1142, Raag Bhairao, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
493._accuracy_note: Partial: both show the weak made strong by where they stand, but the Kural means a tactical position and Gurbani means spiritual shelter.

494.quote_or_event: “My enemies and opponents have grown weary of attacking me, and now, I have become happy, O my friends and Siblings of Destiny.”
494.explanation: In a hymn of thanksgiving, Guru Arjan says that those who set out to harm him have worn themselves out and given up, because he stands under the Lord's protection.
494.tie_back: The Kural says enemies who planned to win drop their plans when the defender holds firm to the right ground; Guru Arjan describes opponents who grew weary and gave up.
494.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 826, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
494._accuracy_note: A good fit on enemies abandoning their attempts; the secure position in Gurbani is divine protection, not well-chosen terrain.

495.quote_or_event: “O mind, love the Lord, as the fish loves the water.”
495.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the fish, which thrives in water and cannot live outside it even for a moment, as an image of the soul's dependence on God.
495.tie_back: The Kural's crocodile is mighty in deep water and helpless on land; Gurbani's fish likewise has its whole life and strength in its own element.
495.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 60, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
495._accuracy_note: The image of a water creature whose strength depends on its element is close; Guru Nanak uses it for love of God, not for military advantage.

496.quote_or_event: “If someone embarks on a boat of stone, he shall drown with its cargo.”
496.explanation: Guru Nanak warns that a vessel unfit for the water sinks with everything aboard, an image for relying on the wrong support to cross the world-ocean.
496.tie_back: The Kural says the chariot cannot run on the sea nor the ship on land; Guru Nanak likewise shows that a means unsuited to its medium brings only ruin.
496.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 420, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
496._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared point is a vehicle unfit for its element, but Guru Nanak's verse is a spiritual warning and does not speak of each thing having its proper field.

497.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else”
497.explanation: In this salok Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the truly wise person as one who neither threatens others nor gives way to fear of them.
497.tie_back: The Kural says that once a plan is complete and the ground is right, fearlessness is the only ally needed; Guru Tegh Bahadur makes fearlessness the mark of the wise.
497.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
497._accuracy_note: Strong on fearlessness as the decisive quality; the Kural ties it to planning and position, which the salok does not mention.

498.quote_or_event: At Chamkaur in December 1705, Guru Gobind Singh, with only a small band of Sikhs, took shelter in a walled, double-storeyed house with a single entrance. He posted eight Sikhs to guard each of its four sides and two at the gate, and through a whole day the much larger imperial army surrounding it failed to storm it.
498.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism describes how a handful of defenders, using a defensible house as a temporary citadel, held off repeated assaults until their arrows and ammunition ran out.
498.tie_back: The Kural says a small force on ground where its strength counts saps the drive of a large army; at Chamkaur a few Sikhs on well-chosen ground held off a far larger host.
498.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Chamkaur Sahib', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
498._accuracy_note: A close historical parallel for a small force holding strong ground; honestly, the defenders were overwhelmed by nightfall and Guru Gobind Singh escaped, so the advantage was real but not decisive.

499.quote_or_event: For much of the eighteenth century, after the death of Guru Gobind Singh, the Sikhs of the Punjab were under threat and siege from both Mughal and Afghan armies, yet they could not be put down in their own land, and from about the 1760s they were the de facto rulers of many parts of the Punjab.
499.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project summarises how a community without great fortresses endured decades of campaigns against it in its home region and eventually came to rule there.
499.tie_back: The Kural says that even people with no strong fort or special strength are hard to beat when attacked in the land where they live; the Sikhs' survival in the Punjab bears this out.
499.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'The Struggle for Survival' (paraphrase)
499._accuracy_note: Next-best: the source describes survival under siege and later rule, but does not itself credit home ground as the reason, so the link to the Kural is partly interpretive.

500.quote_or_event: “Attracted by the lure of sexual desire, the elephant is captured, O crazy mind, and now the halter is placed around its neck.”
500.explanation: Kabir recalls how the mighty elephant is drawn onto ground where it can be trapped, and once caught it must bear the goad and halter.
500.tie_back: The Kural's fearless war elephant is brought down even by jackals once it is stuck in the mire; Kabir's elephant likewise loses all its power once it is lured onto the wrong ground.
500.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 335, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
500._accuracy_note: Partial: both show a powerful elephant made helpless by being caught in the wrong place, but Kabir's point is about desire as a trap, not battlefield terrain.
